prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The

outputs.L1:
The boss is sitting at the desk. The boss does not look at her. The boss is waiting for the black telephone to ring; she is also waiting for a ring from the boss. He is waiting for the files from her, her blue dress wrapped around her body like a reused file folder, her hands clenched tightly around the files. The filing cabinet might eat her, might take her hand off. The boss might eat her. The boss wants her, but the boss wants money more—just a little bit more. The boss always seems to want the money a bit more.

The boss does not hear the taxis outside, waiting for all the women down on the street. Across the street, a boss prepares for bed. Another boss, above him in apartment X, rotates a Q-tip in his ear before sex, despite the instructions on the box.

We took my father out of the paper, the living will. The letters, with their little capes, will leave the paper. Who will take care of my children later? Who will take care of my father? The will will take care of no one. A piece of paper cannot take care of anyone. I cannot take care of everyone.

On some nights, I wake in a panic and cannot tell whether I am dead or alive. This year, I dye my hair so I will not have to die.
outputs.L2: The boss sits behind the desk, not looking at her. He is listening for the black phone to start ringing. She is waiting, too, for a call from him. He is expecting her to bring the files. Her blue dress clings to her like an old file folder wrapped around her. Her fingers grip the papers tightly. The filing cabinet could swallow her, could bite off her hand. The boss could swallow her too. He desires her, but he desires money more—only slightly more, yet always more. He never seems to notice the taxis outside, lined up on the street for all the women below. Across the way, one boss gets ready to sleep. Above him, in apartment X, another boss twists a Q-tip in his ear before sex, ignoring the warning printed on the package. We removed my father from the document, from the living will. The letters, with their tiny capes, will fly off the page. Who will look after my children someday? Who will look after my father? The will cannot protect anyone. A sheet of paper is unable to care for a person. I cannot be responsible for everybody. Some nights I jolt awake terrified, unable to know whether I am living or dead. This year, I color my hair so that I do not have to die.
outputs.L3:
The boss sits at his desk, waiting. He waits for the telephone to ring, for business to arrive, for decisions to be demanded of him. He also waits for the woman to bring him files, as if her movements and her labor are part of the machinery of the office. His desk becomes a place of control and expectation, where communication, paperwork, and authority all converge.

Within this space, the woman feels both threatened and objectified. She is not seen simply as a worker or a person, but as someone the boss desires and uses. His attention turns her into an object, just as his greed turns the office into a place driven by money. The boss wants profit, but he also wants possession. The woman’s discomfort reveals how power in the workplace can become intimate and invasive, shaping not only what people do but how safe they feel in their own bodies.

The scene then broadens beyond this single office. The boss and the woman become part of a larger pattern: other bosses sit at other desks, other women carry other files, and the same relationships of power repeat themselves. The office is no longer just one room but a symbol of a wider world structured by labor, hierarchy, desire, and exploitation. What begins as a private moment becomes social and political, suggesting that these dynamics are not isolated accidents but part of a system.

The speaker then turns inward, reflecting on legal documents such as wills and living wills. These papers are meant to organize care, inheritance, responsibility, and death. They promise clarity and protection, but the speaker recognizes their limits. A document can state wishes, distribute property, or assign authority, yet it cannot love, comfort, or truly care for another person. Paper can record intentions, but it cannot replace human presence or tenderness.

This realization leaves the speaker overwhelmed. Responsibility becomes heavy: the responsibility to prepare, to protect others, to confront illness and mortality, to make decisions before crisis arrives. Panic rises from the awareness that life is fragile and that no amount of paperwork can fully defend against loss. In response, the speaker turns to hair dye, a small but meaningful act of resistance. Dyeing the hair becomes a way to push back against time, aging, and thoughts of death. It is not a solution, but it offers a momentary feeling of control, a way to insist on life and appearance in the face of fear.
outputs.L4:
The text explores the pressures of workplace power, gendered vulnerability, money, mortality, and caregiving through surreal and fragmented imagery. Its world is filled with bosses, files, legal papers, offices, and obligations, but these ordinary institutional objects become strange and threatening. Documents that should organize life instead seem to multiply anxiety. Legal papers that should offer protection feel inadequate. Files, signatures, and bureaucratic procedures appear as fragile barriers against fear, illness, death, and exploitation.

At the center of the text is a speaker who feels exposed within systems that are supposed to provide order. The workplace is not simply a place of employment; it becomes a site where power is unevenly distributed and where the body is made vulnerable. Bosses and authorities appear to control money, time, and security, while the speaker is left navigating uncertainty. This vulnerability is also gendered: the speaker’s fear is tied not only to economic dependence but also to the bodily and emotional risks often placed on women or caregivers. Anxiety is not abstract here. It is physical, intimate, and urgent.

Money moves through the text as both necessity and threat. It represents survival, but it also reveals dependence on institutions that may be indifferent or harmful. The speaker seems aware that financial security can disappear quickly, and that paperwork, employment, or official promises cannot fully shield a person from catastrophe. Mortality presses against these concerns. Death, illness, and bodily fragility interrupt the language of business and law, reminding the reader that human need cannot be reduced to forms, contracts, or administrative systems.

Caregiving also becomes central to the text’s emotional force. The speaker seems to be thinking not only about self-protection but also about responsibility for others. The need to care and be cared for clashes with the coldness of institutional structures. Offices, laws, and documents may claim to manage human life, but they cannot truly provide tenderness, safety, or comfort. The text therefore suggests a deep failure in the systems people are told to trust.

Because of this, the speaker’s panic does not seem irrational. It feels like a response to a world in which the official mechanisms of protection are hollow. The fragmented, surreal style mirrors the speaker’s distress: thoughts break apart, images collide, and ordinary objects become charged with dread. Yet within this panic, the speaker’s small acts of self-preservation become meaningful. Even minor attempts to prepare, resist, organize, or survive feel urgently human. The text ultimately presents a world where institutions cannot adequately care for people, and where the vulnerable must struggle to protect themselves and one another despite that failure.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest and most common words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in how we communicate. It is called a definite article, and it helps us talk about something specific. For example, when we say “a book,” we could mean any book. But when we say “the book,” we are talking about a particular book that the speaker and listener both understand.

Although “the” is simple, it gives clarity and meaning to sentences. It can point to something unique, such as “the sun,” “the moon,” or “the world.” It can also help identify people, places, and objects in everyday conversation. Without “the,” English would sound less natural and more confusing.

In many ways, “the” shows how powerful small words can be. It may not carry much meaning by itself, but when placed in a sentence, it helps organize ideas and guide understanding. This tiny word proves that even the simplest parts of language are essential.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single-paragraph prose poem in a surreal feminist office-noir style, with repeated phrases about “the boss,” a secretary holding files, a black telephone, money, taxis, and then a sudden turn into anxiety about a father’s living will, caretaking, death, and dyed hair.
counterfactuals.output: The boss says the boss is busy, the boss says the boss is a door with a gold nameplate and no room behind it, while the secretary holding files stands under the fluorescent moon like a witness in lipstick, the secretary holding files, the secretary holding files, each folder fat with alibis, pink slips, unpaid prayers; on the desk the black telephone sweats and rings without ringing, the black telephone knows who took the money, who hid the money, who made the money call everyone sweetheart, and outside the rain slicks the street where taxis idle like yellow animals waiting to swallow women whole—taxis for the boss, taxis from the boss, taxis circling the block of the boss’s desire—while I count my wages in bruises and carbon copies, while the secretary holding files whispers that every office is a crime scene if you turn on the lamp; then suddenly the black telephone is my father’s voice, or not his voice but the absence wearing his voice, asking about the living will, the forms, the durable power, the choice no daughter wants notarized, and the boss becomes the doctor, the boss becomes the bedrail, the boss becomes the clock above the nurse’s station, and I am taking taxis to pharmacies, taxis to appointments, taxis through the money-burning dark, caretaking with one hand and signing death into neat little boxes with the other, thinking of his dyed hair, too black, too loyal to the young man he no longer is, shining on the pillow like spilled ink from the secretary’s files, while the black telephone waits in my purse with its mouth open, and the boss, the boss, the boss says nothing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental flash fiction piece with no conventional plot, using obsessive repetition and associative leaps: start with a boss at a desk ignoring a woman in a blue dress, include filing cabinets and telephones, then drift into legal documents, family responsibility, panic, and mortality.
counterfactuals.output:
The boss sat at the desk. The desk was larger than the room, larger than the morning, larger than the woman in the blue dress standing beside it with her hands folded like a petition. The boss did not look up. The boss turned a page. The boss signed a form. The boss lifted the telephone receiver and set it down again without speaking.

The woman in the blue dress waited.

The blue dress waited.

The desk waited in its varnish.

Behind her, filing cabinets stood in rows, gray, green, gray, dented at the corners, full of names and dates and copies of copies and carbon paper ghosts. Each drawer had a small metal mouth. Each mouth had a label. Each label had a number. Each number referred to another number. Each number said: not yet, not now, not yours.

The telephones rang.

One telephone rang on the boss’s desk. One telephone rang in the outer office. One telephone rang in the wall. One telephone rang inside the filing cabinet marked CLAIMS 1978–1982. One telephone rang under the blue dress, inside the hem, where a loose thread trembled like a tiny nerve.

The boss did not look up.

The woman said, “Excuse me.”

The boss signed.

The woman said, “Excuse me.”

The boss turned the page.

The woman said, “It concerns my father.”

The filing cabinets inhaled.

It concerned her father. It concerned her mother. It concerned the dependent minor, the beneficiary, the designated heir, the next of kin, the surviving spouse, the responsible party, the eldest daughter, the one who answered the telephone, the one who knew where the pills were kept, the one who had memorized the difference between regular forms and urgent forms, the one who carried receipts in her purse like damp leaves.

The boss said nothing.

The telephones rang.

A legal document lay on the desk between them. It was not a document but a field of white snow. It was not a field but a hospital sheet. It was not a sheet but a surrender flag. It was titled in bold:

NOTICE OF OBLIGATION.

Below that:

AFFIDAVIT OF CONTINUING RESPONSIBILITY.

Below that:

SIGN HERE.

Below that:

SIGN HERE ALSO.

Below that:

INITIAL.

Below that:

I swear, under penalty, under oath, under the buzzing fluorescent light, under the eyes of clerks and sons and daughters and God if available, that I have read and understood the foregoing, though I have not read it, though I do not understand it, though the words swarm, though the words rearrange themselves into the shape of my father’s hand on the bedrail.

The woman in the blue dress did not cry. The blue dress did not cry. The desk did not cry. The filing cabinets did not cry because they were full.

The boss opened a drawer.

Inside the drawer: paper clips, a stamp pad, a sandwich wrapped in wax paper, three rubber bands, a prescription bottle without a label, a childhood kitchen, a mother saying your father can’t be left alone, a father saying I’m fine, I’m fine, I’m fine, although his slippers were on the wrong feet and the gas was on and the mail was in the freezer.

The boss took out a pen.

The pen was black.

The pen was the color of signatures.

The pen was the color of holes.

“Please,” said the woman.

The word please slid off the desk and fell to the carpet. The carpet accepted it. The carpet had accepted coffee, ash, dust, staples, a single pearl earring, flakes of winter salt, skin, worry, all the little sheddings of people who had come into the office believing offices could answer them.

The telephones rang.

In another room, a telephone rang beside an empty chair.

In another house, a telephone rang beside a pot boiling over.

In another year, a telephone rang and no one answered because the body in the hall had already cooled, because the blue dress was black now, because the cabinets had been emptied into boxes, because the boxes had been carried to a car, because the car had been driven through rain, because rain signs no forms and recognizes no heirs.

The boss said, “There are procedures.”

There are procedures.

There are procedures for grief. Take a number. Complete Section B. Attach proof of relationship. Attach proof of death. Attach proof of life. Attach proof that you did not intend for any of this to happen. Attach the original certificate, not a copy. Copies will not be returned. Fathers will not be returned. Mothers will not be returned. Time will not be returned. Dresses may be dry-cleaned at owner’s risk.

The woman looked at the boss.

The boss looked at the document.

The document looked at the woman.

The filing cabinets leaned closer, but only slightly, because metal must preserve its dignity.

Panic began as a small white animal under her ribs.

It scratched.

It scratched at the legal language. It scratched at the word obligation. It scratched at continuing. Continuing responsibility. Continuing. Continuing. The father continuing to fall. The mother continuing to call. The rent continuing. The medicine continuing. The body continuing until it doesn’t. The telephone continuing after the body doesn’t. The boss continuing to sign. The pen continuing to move. The drawers continuing to close with the sound of small verdicts.

“I can’t,” said the woman.

The boss did not look up.

“I can’t,” said the blue dress.

The filing cabinets answered in alphabetical order.

A through D: You can.

E through H: You must.

I through M: You already have.

N through R: Failure to comply.

S through Z: Consequences.

The fluorescent light hummed like a trapped insect, like a priest clearing his throat, like the dial tone after bad news. The woman thought of her father’s shoes. She thought of envelopes on the kitchen table. She thought of the way responsibility arrives not as a commandment burning on stone but as a telephone call at 6:17 p.m. saying he’s wandered again, saying she’s fallen again, saying we found him, saying we need you to come, saying are you the daughter, saying are you authorized, saying are you aware, saying hello, hello, hello.

The boss stamped the document.

DENIED.

Or perhaps:

RECEIVED.

The difference was a matter of ink.

The boss stamped again.

The stamp came down like a heart.

The stamp came down like a shovel.

The stamp came down like a door.

The woman in the blue dress saw then that the desk was not a desk but a coffin with drawers. The filing cabinets were not filing cabinets but apartment buildings for the dead, each folder a rented room, each label a name that had once answered when called. The telephones were not telephones but black flowers blooming from every surface, ringing and ringing for those who had gone too far down the corridor to hear.

The boss still did not look up.

Perhaps the boss was dead.

Perhaps the boss had always been dead.

Perhaps everyone in the office had died years ago and continued out of habit: signing, stamping, filing, calling, being called, ignoring the woman in the blue dress because to look at her would be to admit that she had entered the same machinery, the same slow cabinet, the same obligation to become paper.

The woman placed her hand on the desk.

The desk was cold.

The desk had a pulse.

The pulse said: sign here.

The pulse said: daughter.

The pulse said: until.

The telephones rang.

The woman picked up the nearest receiver. She meant to say hello. She meant to say I am here. She meant to say I have done everything. She meant to say I am afraid my father will die. She meant to say I am afraid my mother will die. She meant to say I am afraid I will die before anyone looks up.

But the line was already speaking.

A voice said, “This call may be recorded.”

A voice said, “For quality assurance.”

A voice said, “Please hold.”

And she held.

She held the receiver.

She held the document.

She held the family.

She held the blue dress around her knees.

She held the room as it filled with ringing.

She held and held and held until holding became her name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the style of contemporary fragmented prose poetry, blending workplace power dynamics, sexual tension, capitalism, apartment voyeurism, and grief over a parent’s living will; avoid line breaks and use a breathless run-on sentence structure.
counterfactuals.output: In the glass office where everyone can see everyone pretending not to be seen, my manager says circle back and I feel his hand not touching the small charged weather above my shoulder, the spreadsheet blinking like a city of little rented rooms, each cell a window, each window a debt, and across the courtyard at night the woman in 6B eats standing up in her bra while the man behind her practices being absent, and I watch because watching is cheaper than therapy, cheaper than love, cheaper than calling my father’s lawyer to ask what exactly “no extraordinary measures” means when ordinary has always meant pain with fluorescent lighting, ordinary has meant my mother’s signature trembling at the bottom of a document that speaks in the cool voice of a hospital administrator, and in the morning the CEO says family during the all-hands and the stock price rises like a fever nobody can afford to treat, and my manager leans over my chair to correct the margin on a deck about growth and I become all margin, all corrected, all animal heat under a blouse bought on clearance, while downstairs the lobby orchids bloom under rented light and the security guard says have a good one as if one is a thing we are issued at birth and then spend, spend, spend, and I think of my mother folding towels even after the diagnosis, making neat squares of the future, saying don’t let them keep me if I’m not there, as if there is a there to remain in, as if the body is an apartment you can sublet after the tenant has gone quiet, and across the courtyard 6B turns off her lamp and becomes a negative space I fill with projections, bonuses, severance, the soft porn of other people’s routines, while my inbox reproduces like mold and desire wears a badge clipped to its belt and capitalism keeps asking if I have bandwidth, if I can take ownership, if I can make a deck from the raw material of my dread, and somewhere a ventilator practices its mechanical psalm, and somewhere a notary’s stamp comes down like a gavel on mercy, and I am still at my desk after dark, watching my reflection float over the city, wanting to be touched and not managed, seen and not audited, loved and not optimized, wanting my mother to live and also not suffer, which is the most expensive contradiction, the one no benefits portal can contain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a strange, unsettling paragraph about an office scene where the boss wants money more than the woman, the files feel dangerous, taxis wait outside, other bosses are in nearby apartments, and the narrator ends by reflecting on who will care for their children and father.
counterfactuals.output: The office breathed under the fluorescent lights, its walls sweating the smell of old paper and metal drawers, and the boss sat behind his desk looking not at the woman in the chair but past her, toward the safe, toward the figures in the ledger, wanting money with a hunger more naked than desire. The files lay stacked between them like sleeping animals with teeth, each folder too heavy with names, debts, and signatures to touch without fear. Outside, taxis waited in a yellow row along the curb, engines ticking softly as if they had been summoned for an evacuation no one had announced. In the apartments across the street, other bosses moved behind curtains, drinking, listening, making decisions in rooms that seemed too close to this one. And I stood there, holding my breath, thinking not of escape but of the children, of my father, of who would feed them, wash them, lift them from bed when the morning came without us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense avant-garde monologue that moves from a secretary and her boss to urban nightlife, apartment interiors, legal papers, family caregiving, and fear of death, using repetition of “the boss” and “the will” and ending with hair dye as a way to avoid dying.
counterfactuals.output:
The secretary says the boss and the boss says coffee and the coffee says nine-thirty and the clock says no, not yet, not ever, because time is only a typist with bitten nails copying the same memo into different skins. The boss enters in his gray arithmetic, the boss enters with his cufflinks like tiny subpoenas, the boss enters smelling of rain on money, and the secretary, whose name has been filed under miscellaneous, lifts her face from the carbon paper and sees in him not a man but a corridor: fluorescent, managerial, without windows.

The boss dictates. The boss paces. The boss says, Take this down. The boss says, In the event of my incapacity. The boss says, Beneficiary. The boss says, residual estate. The boss says, my wife, my former wife, my daughter, my minor son, my holdings, my shares, my body, my instructions. The secretary types the will. The will. The will. The will is a white room where everyone waits to be mentioned. The will is a mouth full of relatives. The will is the boss lying down before he is dead and distributing his pockets to the living.

At five the city removes its office face and powders itself with neon. The secretary walks out with the will still clacking in her wrists. The streets open like wet mouths. Bars bloom blue. Taxis slide by, yellow fish with exhausted hearts. Girls in silver boots smoke beside black doors. Men laugh into telephones as if laughing could extend the lease. Somewhere a saxophone is being strangled beautifully. Somewhere a bottle breaks and becomes a constellation. The boss is in every window, reflected and multiplied: the boss drinking gin, the boss buying orchids, the boss touching the sleeve of a woman young enough to be an error in the document.

The night says sign here. The city says initial here. The body says witness me.

In apartments above the laundromats, chairs crouch around tables. A lamp wears its shade like a bandage. Someone has left soup congealing on the stove, a spoon upright in it like a small metallic tree. The secretary goes home to her mother’s room, where the air is thick with talcum, pills, old roses, and the television’s blue anesthesia. Mother calls from the bed. Mother says water. Mother says lift me. Mother says don’t leave. Mother says who were you before you became my hands?

The will is in the secretary’s bag. The will rustles when she bends to change the sheets. The will rustles when she counts the tablets. The will rustles when she rinses the bedpan, when she folds the quilt, when she answers the phone and says yes, Mr. Hardwick, yes, the boss, yes, first thing in the morning. The will knows all about inheritance but nothing about sponge baths. The will knows silver, acreage, trustees, codicils, but not the hot shame of lifting a mother’s thigh, not the midnight cough, not the daughter’s back burning like a struck match.

The boss has a mother somewhere too, perhaps in a framed photograph, perhaps already translated into jewelry. The boss has children waiting to become clauses. The boss has a wife who will learn him by paragraph. The boss has fear behind his teeth. The boss has hired language to stand between him and the dark.

And the secretary, after mother sleeps, sits at the kitchen table beneath the unreliable bulb and spreads the legal papers before her like bandages for a wound too official to bleed. Testament. Affidavit. Executor. Assets. Death certificate not yet born. She sees the future arrive in triplicate. She sees the apartment after. Empty bed. Two cups. One voice removed from the walls. She sees herself becoming the leftover daughter, the unmarried drawer, the emergency contact, the woman with sensible shoes and a purse full of receipts, keys, prescriptions, the will, the will, the will.

Outside, the city keeps dying in public and calling it nightlife. Lipstick on glasses. Music in basements. Leather jackets. Steam from grates. The moon like a pill no one can swallow. Everyone dancing under the temporary pardon of electric light. Everyone saying not me, not yet, another round, another song, another body pressed to mine in the dark.

But death is a clerk too. Death takes dictation. Death says name. Death says date. Death says next of kin. Death says the boss. Death says the mother. Death says the secretary. Death says the will. Death says there is no carbon copy you can keep.

In the bathroom mirror her face floats above the sink, pale as an unsigned page. Gray at the roots, those little legal threads, those witnesses for the prosecution. She opens the cabinet. Tubes, gloves, a plastic bottle of brown-black promise. She mixes the chemicals like an alchemist of postponement, paints the night back into her hair, stains the evidence, erases the affidavit of age strand by strand, because if the boss can write the will, if the will can pretend to master death, then she can stand under the buzzing bulb with dye running down her temples and refuse the verdict, refuse the body’s filed memorandum, refuse the grave’s appointment, and not die, not die, not die, not while the color takes, not while the hair darkens, not while hair dye remains a way to avoid dying.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
